newsitem.title: UK: Oil rallies on rumours, but still well supplied.
newsitem.headline: Oil rallies on rumours, but still well supplied.

text.p: World oil prices rallied late on Thursday as dealers seized upon unsubstantiated rumours of a problem at a U.S refinery to push the market higher.
Concern over the possibility of increasing Middle Eastern tension also aided the move up, but the market remains fundamentally well supplied.

World benchmark Brent Blend crude oil for June delivery was up 35 cents at $18.42 a barrel at the close of business having spent much of the day trading in a narrow band between $18.05 and $18.22 on London's International Petroleum Exchange (IPE).

Traders said the longer term fundamentals of a market sitting on comfortable supplies and stocks had not changed, but that concern over Iranian war-games, Kuwaiti complaints to the United Nations about Iraqi attacks on two navy ships, and BBC reports quoting Iraqi Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) radio that United Nations oil monitors had been arrested had prompted oil traders to err on the side of caution.
The United Nations said it had no knowledge that any of its personnel had been detained.
Michael Rothman, senior energy analyst at Merrill Lynch in New York said.

"With OPEC not seemingly prepared to do anything to reduce their production, short of buyers not lifting oil, the markets are not subject to any upward pressure in the near to medium term unless there were to be some sort of significant geopolitical disturbance,".

"Some experts now talk of 'sanctions fatigue' among the international community, with several states keen to do business with the country. Iraqi oil is also popular with refiners," brokers GNI said in a daily market report.

Iraq's oil minister was in Rome on Thursday announcing a post-sanctions line-up of foreign oil firms to develop Iraqi oil fields and raise the country's production capacity once the U.N. ban is lifted.

He said Iraq was close to a deal on development of the Nasiriya oil field with Italy's Agip. He also said a deal was close with China for developing another oil field as part of plans to raise output capacity to six million barrels per day (bpd) compared with 2.5 million bpd currently and pre-Gulf War capacity of 3.5 million bpd.

Rasheed also said Iraq exported 750,000 barrels per day (bpd) of crude oil last week under the United Nations limited oil sales plan. He told a news conference the export figure compared with some 500,000 bpd last December when the oil-for-food plan began.

The U.N. plan allows Iraq to sell crude oil up to a value of $2 billion over six months to buy food and medicines. The return of Iraqi crude oil to the market for the first time since the August 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait was partly responsible for the decline in oil prices, which in January touched $25 a barrel before falling back on the weight of supply and rising industry stocks.
OPEC is producing nearly two million bpd above its self-imposed ceiling of 25.03 million bpd, which makes provision for Iraqi exports.
